text.title: Counterparts
text.author: James Joyce
text.description: A Dublin clerk named Farrington endures humiliation at work, finds momentary triumph through a witty retort, spends his evening drinking with friends, loses a strength competition, and returns home to brutalize his young son.

rootSpan.title: Counterparts
rootSpan.description: A Dublin clerk named Farrington endures humiliation at work, finds momentary triumph through a witty retort, spends his evening drinking with friends, loses a strength competition, and returns home to brutalize his young son.

childSpans.title: The Office
childSpans.description: Farrington is summoned by Mr Alleyne and endures a tirade of abuse about unfinished work and excessive lunch breaks.

childSpans.title: Summons and Confrontation
childSpans.description: Miss Parker relays Mr Alleyne's demand; Farrington goes upstairs to face his employer's accusations.

childSpans.title: The Bell Rings
childSpans.description: Miss Parker receives a call through the tube from Mr Alleyne demanding Farrington.

childSpans.title: Farrington Ascends
childSpans.description: Farrington climbs the stairs to Mr Alleyne's office, physically described as tall and bulky.

childSpans.title: Mr Alleyne's Tirade
childSpans.description: Mr Alleyne berates Farrington about the unfinished contract and excessive lunch breaks.

childSpans.title: Dismissal and Thirst
childSpans.description: Farrington is dismissed and returns to his desk, feeling rage and thirst.

childSpans.title: Rage and Thirst
childSpans.description: Farrington stares at Mr Alleyne's head, gripped by rage and thirst, contemplating a night of drinking.

childSpans.title: Escape to O'Neill's
childSpans.description: Farrington leaves the office and enters O'Neill's pub for a drink.

childSpans.title: Return and Humiliation
childSpans.description: Farrington returns to the office, is rebuked by Mr Alleyne about missing letters, and delivers a witty retort that astounds everyone.

childSpans.title: Return to Office
childSpans.description: Farrington re-enters the office and is questioned by the chief clerk about his absence.

childSpans.title: Farrington Returns
childSpans.description: Farrington comes back to the office after his drink, assuming an air of absent-mindedness.

childSpans.title: Chief Clerk's Interrogation
childSpans.description: The chief clerk questions Farrington about his absence and assigns him to fetch correspondence.

childSpans.title: Miss Delacour's Visit
childSpans.description: Farrington delivers correspondence to Mr Alleyne's room where Miss Delacour is present.

childSpans.title: Miss Delacour
childSpans.description: Farrington observes Miss Delacour in Mr Alleyne's room and delivers the correspondence.

childSpans.title: Accusation and Retort
childSpans.description: Mr Alleyne accuses Farrington of losing letters; Farrington delivers a witty retort that shocks everyone.

childSpans.title: The Accusation
childSpans.description: Mr Alleyne publicly accuses Farrington of losing two letters from the Delacour case.

childSpans.title: The Witty Retort
childSpans.description: Farrington responds with a clever remark that astounds the office and makes Miss Delacour smile.

childSpans.title: The Evening Out
childSpans.description: Farrington pawns his watch, meets friends at various pubs, encounters an attractive woman, and competes in a strength contest.

childSpans.title: Aftermath and Escape
childSpans.description: Farrington apologizes to Mr Alleyne and leaves the office, contemplating his situation.

childSpans.title: Forced Apology
childSpans.description: Farrington is forced to offer an abject apology to Mr Alleyne for his impertinence.

childSpans.title: The Pawn
childSpans.description: Farrington pawns his watch at Terry Kelly's for six shillings.

childSpans.title: Davy Byrne's Pub
childSpans.description: Farrington meets Nosey Flynn, O'Halloran, and Paddy Leonard at Davy Byrne's and recounts his retort.

childSpans.title: Nosey Flynn
childSpans.description: Farrington encounters Nosey Flynn and tells him the story of his retort.

childSpans.title: O'Halloran and Leonard
childSpans.description: O'Halloran and Paddy Leonard arrive and hear the story; Higgins joins them.

childSpans.title: The Scotch House
childSpans.description: The group moves to the Scotch House where they meet Weathers, an acrobat, and encounter an attractive woman.

childSpans.title: Weathers Arrives
childSpans.description: Leonard introduces the group to Weathers, a performer at the Tivoli.

childSpans.title: The Woman in the Hat
childSpans.description: Farrington becomes fascinated by an attractive woman with a peacock-blue scarf and yellow gloves.

childSpans.title: Mulligan's and the Strength Contest
childSpans.description: The group moves to Mulligan's where Farrington competes in a strength contest with Weathers and loses twice.

childSpans.title: Mulligan's Parlour
childSpans.description: The group enters Mulligan's back parlour and continues drinking.

childSpans.title: The Strength Contest
childSpans.description: Farrington and Weathers engage in a trial of strength; Weathers wins both rounds.

childSpans.title: Return Home
childSpans.description: Farrington returns home humiliated and angry, and brutally beats his young son.

childSpans.title: Journey Home
childSpans.description: Farrington waits for the tram and reflects on his humiliation and lack of money.

childSpans.title: Waiting for the Tram
childSpans.description: Farrington stands at O'Connell Bridge waiting for the Sandymount tram, full of anger and regret.

childSpans.title: Home and Confrontation
childSpans.description: Farrington arrives home to find the kitchen empty and the fire out; he confronts his young son.

childSpans.title: Arrival Home
childSpans.description: Farrington arrives home and finds the kitchen empty with the fire nearly out.

childSpans.title: The Beating
childSpans.description: Farrington beats his young son Tom with a walking-stick for letting the fire out.

farrington.name: Farrington
farrington.description: A Dublin clerk in his middle years, tall and bulky with a dark wine-coloured face, fair eyebrows and moustache. He works at Crosbie & Alleyne and endures constant humiliation from his employer. He is prone to drinking, has a quick wit, and is capable of sudden violence.
farrington.context: A working-class Dubliner in the early 20th century, representing the frustrations of office workers under harsh management.

data.physicalDescription: Tall and of great bulk. Hanging face, dark wine-coloured, with fair eyebrows and moustache. Eyes bulge forward slightly with dirty whites. Inflamed face the colour of dark wine or dark meat.

mr-alleyne.name: Mr Alleyne
mr-alleyne.description: A small man wearing gold-rimmed glasses on a clean-shaven face. He is Farrington's employer and a partner in Crosbie & Alleyne. He is imperious, demanding, and prone to violent outbursts. He has a piercing North of Ireland accent.
mr-alleyne.context: Represents the oppressive management class in Edwardian Dublin.

data.physicalDescription: A little man wearing gold-rimmed glasses on a clean-shaven face. Head is so pink and hairless it seems like a large egg reposing on papers. Mouth twitches with dwarf's passion.

miss-parker.name: Miss Parker
miss-parker.description: A female clerk at Crosbie & Alleyne who operates the telephone tube and types correspondence.
miss-parker.context: A working woman in an office environment.

mr-shelley.name: Mr Shelley
mr-shelley.description: The chief clerk at Crosbie & Alleyne. He is observant and somewhat sympathetic to Farrington, though he maintains professional distance.
mr-shelley.context: A middle-ranking office worker in Edwardian Dublin.

miss-delacour.name: Miss Delacour
miss-delacour.description: A middle-aged woman of Jewish appearance who visits Mr Alleyne's office frequently. She is described as stout and amiable, and is rumoured to be the object of Mr Alleyne's affections or interest in her money.
miss-delacour.context: A woman of means in Edwardian Dublin society.

data.physicalDescription: Middle-aged woman of Jewish appearance. Stout amiable person. Wears a great black feather in her hat and carries an umbrella.

nosey-flynn.name: Nosey Flynn
nosey-flynn.description: One of Farrington's drinking companions. He sits in his usual corner at Davy Byrne's and is impressed by Farrington's retort.
nosey-flynn.context: A Dublin working-class man and regular at public houses.

paddy-leonard.name: Paddy Leonard
paddy-leonard.description: One of Farrington's drinking companions. He is present at Davy Byrne's, the Scotch House, and Mulligan's.
paddy-leonard.context: A Dublin working-class man and regular at public houses.

o-halloran.name: O'Halloran
o-halloran.description: One of Farrington's drinking companions. He is present at Davy Byrne's, the Scotch House, and Mulligan's. He tells a story of his own retort to a chief clerk.
o-halloran.context: A Dublin working-class man and regular at public houses.

higgins.name: Higgins
higgins.description: A colleague of Farrington's at the office who is present at Davy Byrne's. He imitates Mr Alleyne's manner of shaking his fist.
higgins.context: A Dublin office worker and drinking companion.

weathers.name: Weathers
weathers.description: A young acrobat and knockabout artiste performing at the Tivoli. He is introduced to Farrington's group at the Scotch House and later defeats Farrington in a strength contest at Mulligan's.
weathers.context: A theatrical performer in Edwardian Dublin.

data.occupation: acrobat and artiste at the Tivoli
data.physicalDescription: Young man with strong biceps. Complexion changes to peony during exertion.

woman-in-hat.name: Woman in the Hat
woman-in-hat.description: An attractive young woman encountered at Mulligan's. She wears a peacock-blue muslin scarf and bright yellow gloves. She speaks with a London accent and brushes against Farrington's chair.
woman-in-hat.context: A woman from the Tivoli theatrical company.

data.physicalDescription: Striking appearance. Immense scarf of peacock-blue muslin wound round her hat and knotted in a great bow under her chin. Bright yellow gloves reaching to the elbow. Plump arm moved with much grace. Large dark brown eyes with oblique staring expression.

curate.name: Curate
curate.description: A man working at O'Neill's pub who serves Farrington a glass of plain porter. Later appears at Mulligan's standing beside the strength contest table.

tom.name: Tom
tom.description: Farrington's young son. A little boy who comes running down the stairs when Farrington arrives home. He is beaten by his father with a walking-stick.
tom.context: A child in a working-class Dublin household.

ada.name: Ada
ada.description: Farrington's wife. A little sharp-faced woman who bullies her husband when he is sober and is bullied by him when he is drunk. She is out at the chapel when Farrington arrives home.
ada.context: A working-class Dublin woman and mother.

mr-crosbie.name: Mr Crosbie
mr-crosbie.description: A partner in Crosbie & Alleyne, mentioned as a threat by Mr Alleyne if work is not completed.
mr-crosbie.context: A business owner in Edwardian Dublin.

peake.name: Peake
peake.description: A former employee at Crosbie & Alleyne who was hounded out of the office by Mr Alleyne to make room for Mr Alleyne's nephew.
peake.context: A victim of Mr Alleyne's management style.

terry-kelly.name: Terry Kelly
terry-kelly.description: Owner of a pawn-office in Fleet Street where Farrington pawns his watch.

crosbie-alleyne-office.name: Crosbie & Alleyne Office
crosbie-alleyne-office.description: A Dublin office where Farrington works as a clerk. It has a lower office with desks and a counter, and an upper office where Mr Alleyne works. The office contains a tube system for communication, a hat-rack, and gas lighting.

alleyne-office.name: Mr Alleyne's Office
alleyne-office.description: The private office of Mr Alleyne on the second landing of the Crosbie & Alleyne building. It contains a desk with piles of documents and is where Mr Alleyne conducts business and receives visitors.
alleyne-office.context: The inner sanctum of office authority.
alleyne-office.geography: Second landing of Crosbie & Alleyne office building, Dublin

oneills-pub.name: O'Neill's Shop
oneills-pub.description: A pub with a dark snug and a bar. It has a little window that looks into the bar. Farrington enters furtively to drink a glass of plain porter.
textMentions: the dark snug of O'Neill's shop
oneills-pub.context: A Dublin public house in the early 20th century.

eustace-street.name: Eustace Street
eustace-street.description: A Dublin street where the lamps have been lit in the February darkness and fog. Farrington walks along this street returning to the office.
eustace-street.context: A Dublin street in the early 20th century.

temple-bar.name: Temple Bar
temple-bar.description: A narrow alley in Dublin through which Farrington passes on his way to Terry Kelly's pawn-office.
textMentions: the narrow alley of Temple Bar
temple-bar.context: A Dublin street in the early 20th century.

terry-kellys-pawn-office.name: Terry Kelly's Pawn-Office
terry-kellys-pawn-office.description: A pawn-office in Fleet Street where Farrington pawns his watch for six shillings.
textMentions: Terry Kelly's pawn-office in Fleet Street
terry-kellys-pawn-office.context: A Dublin pawn-office in the early 20th century.

westmoreland-street.name: Westmoreland Street
westmoreland-street.description: A Dublin street crowded with young men and women returning from business and ragged urchins selling evening editions.
westmoreland-street.context: A busy Dublin street in the early 20th century.

davy-byrnes.name: Davy Byrne's
davy-byrnes.description: A pub where Nosey Flynn sits in his usual corner. Farrington meets his friends here and recounts his retort to Mr Alleyne.
davy-byrnes.context: A Dublin public house in the early 20th century.

callan-fownes-street.name: Callan's of Fownes's Street
callan-fownes-street.description: A pub where O'Halloran previously made a retort to a chief clerk, mentioned in his story.

duke-street.name: Duke Street
duke-street.description: A Dublin street where Higgins and Nosey Flynn part ways from the other three men.
duke-street.context: A Dublin street in the early 20th century.

ballast-office.name: Ballast Office
ballast-office.description: A Dublin landmark near which Farrington and his companions decide to visit the Scotch House.
ballast-office.context: A Dublin landmark in the early 20th century.

scotch-house.name: The Scotch House
scotch-house.description: A pub full of men and loud with the noise of tongues and glasses. Farrington and his companions meet Weathers here and encounter an attractive woman.
scotch-house.context: A Dublin public house in the early 20th century.

tivoli.name: The Tivoli
tivoli.description: A theatre where Weathers and the woman in the hat perform as acrobats and artistes.
tivoli.context: A Dublin theatre in the early 20th century.

mulligans.name: Mulligan's
mulligans.description: A pub with a parlour at the back where Farrington and his companions continue drinking and where the strength contest takes place.
mulligans.context: A Dublin public house in the early 20th century.

oconnell-bridge.name: O'Connell Bridge
oconnell-bridge.description: A Dublin bridge where Farrington waits for the Sandymount tram to take him home.
oconnell-bridge.context: A Dublin landmark in the early 20th century.

shelbourne-road.name: Shelbourne Road
shelbourne-road.description: A Dublin street where the Sandymount tram lets Farrington down near his home.
shelbourne-road.context: A Dublin street in the early 20th century.

barracks.name: Barracks
barracks.description: A military barracks near Farrington's home, mentioned as he walks along in its shadow.
barracks.context: A Dublin military installation in the early 20th century.

farrington-home.name: Farrington's Home
farrington-home.description: A working-class Dublin home with a kitchen, a side-door entrance, and stairs leading upstairs. The kitchen has a fireplace and chairs.
farrington-home.context: A working-class Dublin household in the early 20th century.

chapel.name: Chapel
chapel.description: A Catholic chapel where Farrington's wife Ada is out at when he arrives home.
chapel.context: A Dublin Catholic chapel in the early 20th century.

dublin.name: Dublin
dublin.description: The city of Dublin, Ireland, where the entire story takes place. It is depicted as a cold, foggy city in February with various pubs, streets, and working-class neighborhoods.
dublin.context: Early 20th century Dublin during the Edwardian era.

contract-bodley-kirwan.name: Contract between Bodley and Kirwan
contract-bodley-kirwan.description: A legal contract that Farrington is supposed to copy. Mr Alleyne demands it be ready by four o'clock. The contract contains the phrase 'In no case shall the said Bernard Bodley be....'
textMentions: the contract between Bodley and Kirwan
contract-bodley-kirwan.context: Office work in an Edwardian law office.
contract-bodley-kirwan.physicalDescription: A contract with multiple pages to be copied
contract-bodley-kirwan.culturalSignificance: Represents the work that Farrington is unable to complete

delacour-correspondence.name: Delacour Correspondence
delacour-correspondence.description: Letters in the Delacour case that Farrington is asked to retrieve. Two letters are missing from the correspondence.
delacour-correspondence.context: Office work in an Edwardian law office.
delacour-correspondence.culturalSignificance: The missing letters become the pretext for Mr Alleyne's public accusation

shepherds-plaid-cap.name: Shepherd's Plaid Cap
shepherds-plaid-cap.description: A cap that Farrington pulls from his pocket and puts on his head when leaving the office to go to O'Neill's pub. He later cramps it back into his pocket when returning.
shepherds-plaid-cap.culturalSignificance: Marks Farrington's furtive departure from the office

glass-plain-porter.name: Glass of Plain Porter
glass-plain-porter.description: A glass of plain porter that Farrington drinks at O'Neill's pub. He drinks it at a gulp.
glass-plain-porter.culturalSignificance: Represents Farrington's thirst and need for escape

caraway-seed.name: Caraway Seed
caraway-seed.description: A caraway seed that Farrington asks for after drinking his glass of plain porter at O'Neill's pub.
caraway-seed.culturalSignificance: A small detail of pub ritual

penny.name: Penny
penny.description: A penny that Farrington puts on the counter at O'Neill's pub to pay for his drink and caraway seed.

umbrella.name: Umbrella
umbrella.description: An umbrella that Miss Delacour carries and smooths the handle of while sitting in Mr Alleyne's office.
umbrella.culturalSignificance: Part of Miss Delacour's refined appearance

black-feather-hat.name: Black Feather Hat
black-feather-hat.description: A hat with a great black feather that Miss Delacour wears. She nods the feather while sitting in Mr Alleyne's office.
textMentions: the great black feather in her hat
black-feather-hat.physicalDescription: A hat with a great black feather
black-feather-hat.culturalSignificance: Part of Miss Delacour's refined appearance

watch.name: Watch
watch.description: Farrington's watch, which he pawns at Terry Kelly's pawn-office for six shillings. He fingers the watch-chain before deciding to pawn it.
watch.culturalSignificance: Represents Farrington's desperation for money and his loss of dignity

coins.name: Six Shillings
coins.description: Six shillings that Farrington receives from pawning his watch. He makes a little cylinder of the coins between his thumb and fingers.
coins.culturalSignificance: Represents Farrington's temporary relief and ability to continue drinking

peacock-blue-scarf.name: Peacock-Blue Muslin Scarf
peacock-blue-scarf.description: An immense scarf of peacock-blue muslin wound round the hat of the attractive woman at Mulligan's, knotted in a great bow under her chin.
textMentions: An immense scarf of peacock-blue muslin
peacock-blue-scarf.physicalDescription: An immense scarf of peacock-blue muslin wound round a hat and knotted in a great bow under the chin
peacock-blue-scarf.culturalSignificance: Part of the woman's striking appearance that fascinates Farrington

yellow-gloves.name: Bright Yellow Gloves
yellow-gloves.description: Bright yellow gloves reaching to the elbow worn by the attractive woman at Mulligan's.
textMentions: bright yellow gloves, reaching to the elbow
yellow-gloves.physicalDescription: Bright yellow gloves reaching to the elbow
yellow-gloves.culturalSignificance: Part of the woman's striking appearance

walking-stick.name: Walking-Stick
walking-stick.description: A walking-stick standing behind the door of Farrington's home that he seizes to beat his son Tom.
walking-stick.context: A household item used as a weapon.
walking-stick.culturalSignificance: Becomes an instrument of violence and child abuse

crosbie-alleyne.name: Crosbie & Alleyne
crosbie-alleyne.description: A Dublin law office with two partners, Mr Crosbie and Mr Alleyne. It employs clerks including Farrington, Miss Parker, and others.
crosbie-alleyne.organizationalStructure: Partners at top, chief clerk, clerks, office staff

farringtons-drinking-circle.name: Farrington's Drinking Circle
farringtons-drinking-circle.description: A group of working-class Dublin men who drink together at various pubs. The group includes Nosey Flynn, Paddy Leonard, O'Halloran, Higgins, and later Weathers.

e01.description: The bell rings furiously and Miss Parker receives a call through the tube from Mr Alleyne demanding that Farrington be sent upstairs.

e02.description: Farrington stands up from his desk, revealing himself to be tall and of great bulk with a hanging face, dark wine-coloured, fair eyebrows and moustache. He lifts the counter and passes by clients, going out of the office with a heavy step.

e03.description: Farrington climbs heavily upstairs to the second landing where Mr Alleyne's office is located. He halts, puffing with labour and vexation, and knocks on the door.

e04.description: Mr Alleyne berates Farrington about the unfinished contract between Bodley and Kirwan, demanding to know why it hasn't been copied by four o'clock. He also criticizes Farrington for taking an hour and a half for lunch instead of half an hour.

e05.description: Farrington stares fixedly at Mr Alleyne's polished skull, gauging its fragility. A spasm of rage grips his throat, then passes, leaving a sharp sensation of thirst. He recognizes the sensation and feels he must have a good night's drinking.

e06.description: Farrington leaves the office, passing the chief clerk Mr Shelley who glances at the hat-rack but sees it complete. On the landing, Farrington pulls a shepherd's plaid cap from his pocket, puts it on, and runs quickly down the rickety stairs. He walks furtively toward the corner and dives into O'Neill's shop.

e07.description: Farrington enters the dark snug of O'Neill's shop, fills up the little window looking into the bar with his inflamed face, and calls out for a glass of plain porter. The curate brings him the drink. He drinks it at a gulp and asks for a caraway seed. He puts his penny on the counter and retreats out of the snug.

e08.description: Farrington returns to the office in the darkness and fog of February. He cramps his cap back into his pocket and re-enters the office, assuming an air of absent-mindedness.

e09.description: The chief clerk Mr Shelley tells Farrington severely that Mr Alleyne has been calling for him and asks where he was. Farrington glances at two male clients at the counter as if to intimate their presence prevents him from answering. The chief clerk laughs and tells Farrington to get a copy of the Delacour correspondence for Mr Alleyne.

e10.description: Farrington goes upstairs to Mr Alleyne's room where he finds Miss Delacour, a middle-aged woman of Jewish appearance, sitting beside Mr Alleyne's desk in an aroma of perfumes. She is smoothing the handle of her umbrella and nodding the great black feather in her hat. Farrington puts the correspondence on the desk and bows respectfully, but neither Mr Alleyne nor Miss Delacour take any notice of his bow.

e11.description: Mr Alleyne and Miss Delacour stand outside the counter while all the clerks turn round in anticipation. Mr Alleyne begins a tirade of abuse, saying that two letters are missing from the Delacour correspondence. Farrington answers that he knows nothing about them and made a faithful copy.

e12.description: Mr Alleyne continues his tirade, asking Farrington if he takes him for a fool. Farrington glances from the lady's face to Mr Alleyne's egg-shaped head and back again, and delivers a witty retort: 'I don't think, sir, that that's a fair question to put to me.'

e13.description: There is a pause in the breathing of the clerks. Everyone is astounded, including the author of the witticism. Miss Delacour, a stout amiable person, begins to smile broadly. Mr Alleyne flushes to the hue of a wild rose and his mouth twitches with dwarf's passion. He shakes his fist in Farrington's face, threatening to make short work of him and demanding an apology or his resignation.

e14.description: Farrington stands in a doorway opposite the office watching to see if the cashier would come out alone. All the clerks pass out and finally the cashier comes out with the chief clerk. Farrington feels his position is bad. He has been obliged to offer an abject apology to Mr Alleyne for his impertinence but knows the office will be a hornet's nest for him.

e15.description: Farrington goes through the narrow alley of Temple Bar quickly, muttering that they can all go to hell because he is going to have a good night of it. He goes to Terry Kelly's pawn-office in Fleet Street. The clerk says 'A crown!' but the consignor holds out for six shillings; in the end six shillings is allowed him. He comes out joyfully, making a little cylinder of the coins between his thumb and fingers.

e16.description: Farrington walks through the crowded Westmoreland Street, looking on the spectacle with proud satisfaction and staring masterfully at office-girls. He preconceives the terms in which he will narrate the incident to the boys. He arrives at Davy Byrne's where Nosey Flynn is sitting in his usual corner. When Flynn hears the story, he stands Farrington a half-one, saying it was as smart a thing as ever he heard.

e17.description: Farrington stands a drink in his turn. After a while O'Halloran and Paddy Leonard come in and the story is repeated to them. O'Halloran stands tailors of malt, hot, all round and tells the story of the retort he had made to the chief clerk when he was in Callan's of Fownes's Street; but he has to admit that it was not as clever as Farrington's retort.

e18.description: Higgins comes in and is asked to give his version of the story. He does so with great vivacity for the sight of five small hot whiskies is very exhilarating. Everyone roars laughing when he shows the way in which Mr Alleyne shook his fist in Farrington's face. Then he imitates Farrington, saying 'And here was my nabs, as cool as you please,' while Farrington looks at the company out of his heavy dirty eyes, smiling.

e19.description: When the round is over, O'Halloran has money but neither of the other two seem to have any; so the whole party leaves the shop somewhat regretfully. At the corner of Duke Street Higgins and Nosey Flynn bevelled off to the left while the other three turned back towards the city. They reach the Ballast Office and Farrington suggests the Scotch House. The bar is full of men and loud with noise. Leonard introduces them to a young fellow named Weathers who is performing at the Tivoli as an acrobat and knockabout artiste.

e20.description: Presently two young women with big hats and a young man in a check suit come in and sit at a table close by. Weathers salutes them and tells the company they are out of the Tivoli. Farrington's eyes wander at every moment in the direction of one of the young women. There is something striking in her appearance. An immense scarf of peacock-blue muslin is wound round her hat and knotted in a great bow under her chin; and she wears bright yellow gloves reaching to the elbow.

e21.description: Farrington gazes admiringly at the plump arm of the woman which she moves very often and with much grace; and when, after a little time, she answers his gaze he admires still more her large dark brown eyes. The oblique staring expression in them fascinates him. She glances at him once or twice and, when the party is leaving the room, she brushes against his chair and says 'O, pardon!' in a London accent. He watches her leave the room in the hope that she would look back at him, but he is disappointed.

e22.description: When Paddy Leonard calls Farrington, he finds that they are talking about feats of strength. Weathers is showing his biceps muscle to the company and boasting so much that the other two have called on Farrington to uphold the national honour. Farrington pulls up his sleeve and shows his biceps muscle. The two arms are examined and compared and finally it is agreed to have a trial of strength. The table is cleared and the two men rest their elbows on it, clasping hands.

e23.description: The trial begins. After about thirty seconds Weathers brings Farrington's opponent's hand slowly down on to the table. Farrington's dark wine-coloured face flushes darker still with anger and humiliation at having been defeated by such a stripling. He protests that Weathers is not playing fair and demands they try again, the best two out of three.

e24.description: The trial begins again. The veins stand out on Farrington's forehead, and the pallor of Weathers' complexion changes to peony. Their hands and arms tremble under the stress. After a long struggle Weathers again brings Farrington's hand slowly on to the table. There is a murmur of applause from the spectators. The curate standing beside the table nods his red head towards the victor and says with stupid familiarity 'Ah! that's the knack!' Farrington turns on the man fiercely, asking what the hell he knows about it.

e25.description: A very sullen-faced Farrington stands at the corner of O'Connell Bridge waiting for the little Sandymount tram to take him home. He is full of smouldering anger and revengefulness. He feels humiliated and discontented; he did not even get drunk; and he has only twopence in his pocket. He curses everything. The tram lets him down at Shelbourne Road and he steers his great body along in the shadow of the wall of the barracks.

e26.description: Farrington goes in by the side-door of his home and finds the kitchen empty and the kitchen fire nearly out. He bawls upstairs 'Ada! Ada!' A little boy comes running down the stairs. Farrington asks who it is, and the boy says 'Me, pa.' Farrington asks if it is Charlie, and the boy says 'No, pa. Tom.' Farrington asks where his mother is, and Tom says she is out at the chapel. Farrington asks if she left any dinner for him.

e27.description: Farrington tells Tom to light the lamp and asks what he means by having the place in darkness. When the lamp is lit, Farrington bangs his fist on the table and shouts 'What's for my dinner?' Tom says he is going to cook it. Farrington jumps up furiously and points to the fire, saying 'On that fire! You let the fire out! By God, I'll teach you to do that again!' He takes a step to the door and seizes the walking-stick. He rolls up his sleeve and begins to beat Tom vigorously with the stick. Tom cries 'O, pa!' and runs whimpering round the table, but Farrington catches him by the coat. Tom falls upon his knees and Farrington strikes at him, saying 'Now, you'll let the fire out the next time! Take that, you little whelp!' Tom utters a squeal of pain as the stick cuts his thigh. He clasps his hands together and cries 'O, pa! Don't beat me, pa! And I'll ... I'll say a Hail Mary for you....'

Formalist Reading.name: Formalist Reading
Formalist Reading.description: A formalist interpretation of 'Counterparts' focusing on narrative structure, linguistic patterns, symbolic imagery, and the formal mechanisms through which Joyce constructs meaning through style, repetition, and structural parallelism.

theme-parallelism-descent.name: Structural Parallelism and Descent
theme-parallelism-descent.description: The story's formal structure mirrors a descent through repeated cycles of humiliation and attempted escape. Each act follows a pattern of confrontation, temporary triumph, and ultimate defeat, creating a formal architecture of cyclical failure.

theme-language-power.name: Language as Power and Impotence
theme-language-power.description: The formal contrast between Farrington's wit (the retort) and his ultimate silence (the beating) demonstrates how language functions as both weapon and illusion. The narrative form emphasizes the gap between linguistic cleverness and actual agency.

theme-physical-description.name: Physical Description as Narrative Determinism
theme-physical-description.description: Joyce's repeated, detailed physical descriptions of Farrington (dark wine-coloured face, bulk, heaviness) function formally to suggest that character is fixed, predetermined, and inescapable. The body becomes a textual prison.

theme-temporal-compression.name: Temporal Compression and Narrative Pace
theme-temporal-compression.description: The formal acceleration of events—from the slow, detailed office scenes to the rapid pub scenes to the violent conclusion—creates a sense of inevitability through pacing itself. Time becomes a formal instrument of fate.

sym-face-wine-coloured.name: The Dark Wine-Coloured Face
sym-face-wine-coloured.description: Farrington's face, repeatedly described as 'dark wine-coloured,' functions as a formal symbol of his intoxication, rage, and fixed identity. The color recurs throughout the narrative, creating a linguistic leitmotif that binds his character to alcohol and violence.

sym-stairs-ascent-descent.name: Stairs and Vertical Movement
sym-stairs-ascent-descent.description: The formal use of stairs—Farrington climbing heavily upstairs to Mr Alleyne's office, then descending, then the final descent home—creates a structural pattern of futile ascent and inevitable descent. Vertical movement becomes a formal expression of social and moral trajectory.

sym-walking-stick.name: The Walking-Stick
sym-walking-stick.description: Formally introduced as a standing object ('standing behind the door'), the walking-stick becomes the instrument through which Farrington's rage finds physical expression. It represents the transformation of linguistic power into bodily violence, completing the narrative's formal arc.

currentMeanings.description: The only form of power Farrington can exercise

sym-thirst-desire.name: Thirst as Formal Motif
sym-thirst-desire.description: Thirst appears formally as both literal (the desire for drink) and metaphorical (unfulfilled desire). The word 'thirst' recurs as a linguistic anchor, creating a formal pattern of perpetual, unsatisfiable longing that structures the narrative.

currentMeanings.description: The gap between aspiration and achievement

symrel-face-thirst.name: Face and Thirst as Linked Motifs
symrel-face-thirst.description: The dark wine-coloured face and the sensation of thirst are formally linked in e05, where rage produces thirst. This symbolic connection suggests that Farrington's physical appearance and his desires are inseparable—his body is his fate.
symrel-face-thirst.nature: Physical form determines psychological and behavioral destiny
symrel-face-thirst.interpretation: Physical form determines psychological and behavioral destiny

symrel-stairs-powerlessness.name: Stairs and Social Powerlessness
symrel-stairs-powerlessness.description: The formal pattern of climbing and descending stairs becomes a symbol of Farrington's inability to escape his social position. Each ascent is followed by humiliation, each descent by further degradation.
symrel-stairs-powerlessness.nature: Vertical movement formalizes the impossibility of social mobility
symrel-stairs-powerlessness.interpretation: Vertical movement formalizes the impossibility of social mobility

symrel-stick-language.name: Walking-Stick as Failed Language
symrel-stick-language.description: The walking-stick represents the formal transformation of Farrington's linguistic wit into physical violence. Where language fails to sustain power, the body takes over—the stick becomes the only language Farrington can speak with authority.
symrel-stick-language.nature: When rhetoric fails, violence becomes the only remaining form of expression and control
symrel-stick-language.interpretation: When rhetoric fails, violence becomes the only remaining form of expression and control

narrator.name: Third-Person Limited Narrator
narrator.description: The narrator maintains a formally detached, third-person perspective that closely follows Farrington's consciousness while preserving ironic distance. The narrator's style—precise, detailed, occasionally sardonic—creates a formal tension between sympathy and judgment.

reader.name: Formalist Reader
reader.description: The reader is positioned to recognize and trace formal patterns: repetitions, structural parallels, linguistic motifs, and symbolic recurrences. The reading experience is one of recognizing how form itself—not just content—generates meaning and inevitability.

author.name: James Joyce
author.description: Joyce as a formal innovator constructing meaning through precise language, structural parallelism, and symbolic imagery. The author's control over style, pacing, and narrative structure is the primary vehicle of meaning.

e01.note: Initiates the formal pattern of summons and confrontation; establishes the hierarchical structure through the tube system

e02.note: Introduces the key physical description (dark wine-coloured face, bulk) that becomes a formal leitmotif throughout the narrative

e03.note: Establishes the vertical movement pattern (ascending stairs) that will be formally repeated and inverted throughout the story

e04.note: Demonstrates the formal structure of accusation and humiliation; establishes Mr Alleyne's rhetorical dominance

e05.note: Formally links physical description (face) with psychological state (thirst); introduces the key motif of thirst that structures desire throughout the narrative

e06.note: Formalizes the pattern of escape and deception; the shepherd's plaid cap becomes a symbol of disguise and evasion

e07.note: Demonstrates the formal structure of quick satisfaction followed by return; establishes the pub as a recurring setting

e08.note: Completes the formal cycle of escape and return; the fog and darkness are formal atmospheric elements

e09.note: Demonstrates Farrington's use of silence and implication as rhetorical strategy; minor formal significance

e10.note: Introduces Miss Delacour as a formal catalyst; her presence triggers the accusation that leads to the retort

e11.note: Establishes the formal structure of public accusation; the missing letters become a pretext for humiliation

e12.note: The witty retort is the formal climax of the office section; represents the peak of Farrington's linguistic power and the moment of greatest formal tension

e13.note: Formally demonstrates the consequences of the retort; the pause in breathing creates a formal moment of suspension before reversal

e14.note: Completes the formal cycle of triumph and defeat; establishes the pattern that will repeat in the evening section

e15.note: Formally represents the transformation of material goods into currency for pleasure; the pawn transaction enables the evening's events

e16.note: Demonstrates the formal repetition of the retort narrative; Farrington becomes a narrator of his own triumph, creating a formal doubling

e17.note: Establishes the formal pattern of competitive storytelling; O'Halloran's inferior retort emphasizes Farrington's superiority in this domain

e18.note: Higgins' imitation creates a formal doubling and tripling of the retort narrative; the repetition emphasizes its centrality to Farrington's identity

e19.note: Introduces Weathers as a formal counterpart to Farrington; establishes the setting for the strength contest

e20.note: Introduces the woman in the hat with detailed formal description; her appearance becomes a formal distraction from the strength contest

e21.note: Demonstrates Farrington's gaze and desire; the woman's London accent and gesture create formal irony (she is unattainable)

e22.note: Formally establishes the strength contest as a parallel to the linguistic contest; both are tests of masculine power

e23.note: The first strength contest defeat is formally significant; Farrington's rage and humiliation mirror his response to Mr Alleyne's accusations

e24.note: The second defeat is formally crucial; the repetition emphasizes the pattern of failure, and the curate's comment triggers Farrington's violence

e25.note: Formally represents the nadir before the final descent; Farrington's emotional state (smouldering anger, humiliation) is formally described in detail

e26.note: Establishes the domestic setting and introduces Tom; the empty kitchen and cold fire are formal symbols of domestic neglect

e27.note: The beating is the formal climax of the entire narrative; it completes the pattern of displaced violence and represents the transformation of linguistic power into bodily domination
